intro: Rachmaninoff was nineteen when he added the Sérénade to his Op. 3 pieces; here he plays it for Victor in 1922. A hushed Sostenuto gives way to a waltz that thins out into quiet chords before one last loud chord.
question: How can a melody sing over a waltz accompaniment without being pushed along by it?

cues.title: How little there is
cues.text: The Sostenuto is marked pp, in 3/8: an F in the left hand, small turning figures around it, and long rests between them. The waltz does not start for nearly a minute.
cues.evidence: The Piano Street scan of the 1892 version shows Sostenuto, pp, 3/8, a left-hand F, sixteenth-note turns and rests in the first system. The analysis puts the opening among the quietest stretches (0:00 and 0:45–0:55) with 0.4–2.6 attacks per second. https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/morceaux-de-fantaisie/serenade-op-3-no-5.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A fifth piece, written fast
cues.text: Rachmaninoff planned four pieces for Op. 3. After reading Tchaikovsky’s newspaper praise of younger composers in November 1892, he said he sat down and composed a fifth: this Sérénade. Gutheil published the set in February 1893.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s note for Hyperion CDA66081 quotes Rachmaninoff on adding the Serenade after Tchaikovsky’s interview and dates publication to February 1893: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: The waltz begins
cues.text: Around 0:56 the level jumps by about ten decibels and attacks rise from about 2.6 to 4.4 a second. In Tempo di Valse a bass note falls on the first beat, with chords on the others, under a melody built from small turns.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −23.4 dB at 0:55 to −13.5 dB at 1:00, attacks from 2.6 to 4.4 per second, and the boundary strength of 0.90 at 0:56 is the second-highest in the file. The score places Tempo di Valse at the end of its first page.

cues.title: Tune against a steady pattern
cues.text: Follow the melody, made of small turning figures, above the regular bass-and-chord pattern. Because the accompaniment is steady, any stretching or pressing of the tune stands out against it.
cues.evidence: The score keeps a bass note and chords in the left hand through the Tempo di Valse; the analysis shows steady attack density (3.2–4.4 per second) from 1:00 to 1:30. This is a listening suggestion, not a measurement of the rubato.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Four takes thrown away
cues.text: Victor’s ledger shows three takes on 1 November 1922 and two on 4 November, all in New York. Only the fifth was kept. A ledger entry for 1 November reads “Steinway piano, style B-211833”.
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix B-27110 lists takes 1–3 (1 November) and 4–5 (4 November 1922) in New York, takes 1–4 destroyed and take 5 as master, and quotes the ledger note on the Steinway: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/800001056/B-27110-Serenade

cues.title: Not the page, the performance
cues.text: Henle’s 2022 critical report says that Rachmaninoff’s own recording of the Sérénade departs from the printed notation of this version “in many places”. It does not say which of his recordings it means, so listen to his choices rather than expecting a literal reading of the score.
cues.evidence: Dominik Rahmer’s comment on Sérénade bars 103–104 (Henle Urtext HN 1491 critical report): https://www.henle.de/media/76/20/d9/1697725714/1491-1697725714-sync.pdf. The report does not identify the recording or the differences, and no comparison with this record has been made.

cues.title: Revised, and played as played
cues.text: In 1940 Rachmaninoff revised the Sérénade; Charles Foley’s edition is headed “Revised and as played by the composer”. This 1922 record is eighteen years older, and Wikipedia’s list of his recordings gives it as the 1892 version.
cues.evidence: Foley’s title page and 1940 date are transcribed in the Henle critical report (https://www.henle.de/media/76/20/d9/1697725714/1491-1697725714-sync.pdf). Wikipedia’s list of the composer’s recordings labels the 4 November 1922 recording the 1892 version: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Rachmaninoff_recordings

cues.title: Back to hush, then one chord
cues.text: The closing pages fall to ppp and pppp, as quiet as the opening. The score ends on one ff chord under a fermata; here the level drops near 2:45–2:50, the closing minute’s loudest window comes at about 2:55, and the sound has gone by 3:05.
cues.evidence: The score’s last systems show ppp and pppp chords and a final ff chord with a fermata. The analysis shows the level falling to −21.9 and −24.3 dB at 2:45 and 2:50, the closing minute’s loudest window at 2:55 (−10.3 dB; 1:15 at −8.4 dB is louder) and silence from 3:05.

transitions.title: Quiet chords, a rising run, then the waltz
transitions.how: The Sostenuto ends on soft chords marked ppp. A short rising run in the bass clef leads into Tempo di Valse, which opens on a rest and then sets a single bass note against light chords in 3/8. The opening’s left hand keeps returning to F, the dominant of B♭ minor; the waltz settles on B♭ minor with a steady bass. Tempo and texture change at once, while the same small turning figures carry over into the melody.
transitions.evidence: The score’s first page ends with ppp chords, a rising run and Tempo di Valse marked p. The analysis shows the largest early jump in level and attack density at 0:56 (−23.4 to −13.5 dB; 2.6 to 4.4 attacks per second), and local key estimates move from F minor (0:00–0:30) to B♭ minor (from 1:00). Key estimates only confirm what the score shows.

transitions.title: The waltz thins to recalled chords
transitions.how: The waltz bass-and-chord pattern falls away. Chords marked ppp and then pppp are as quiet as the opening Sostenuto. The score finishes on a single ff chord under a fermata: the quietest writing in the piece leads straight into its loudest chord, and nothing follows it.
transitions.evidence: The score’s last two systems show ppp and pppp chords and a final ff chord with a fermata. The analysis finds the boundary at 2:44 (strength 0.66) with attack density falling from 4.2 to 2.0 per second and level to −21.9 dB at 2:45, then the loudest window of the closing minute at 2:55.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original (1892) version of the Sérénade, as played by the composer in 1922; performing text not identified
fields.note: Wikipedia’s list of the composer’s recordings labels the 4 November 1922 recording the 1892 version, and the 1940 revised version was published only in 1940 (Henle). IMSLP’s page says No. 5 was revised in 1922; the Henle report documents the revised text as Charles Foley’s 1940 edition, so that remark is not followed. Henle also states that the composer’s own recording diverges from the printed notation of the original version in many places. Henle does not identify which composer recording it means; the cited original score is therefore not assumed to be a literal transcript of the 1922 performance.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: DAHR’s approved take 5 is dated 4 November 1922; takes 1–3 were made on 1 November. The Archive filename and the RCA register give the same date for the reissued track.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Victor 66129 and 816, recorded 1922).
fields.note: DAHR’s catalogue records for Victor 66129 and 816 give a publication date of [1922], and an Internet Archive digitisation of Victrola 66129 gives 1922; both are catalogue-derived years, not release days. The 1925 Victor catalogue lists the Serenade (Op. 3, No. 5) coupled with the Minuet from L’Arlésienne, which establishes publication no later than 1925 independently of the session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
